newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Chirac lavishes praise on Clinton.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac lavishes praise on Clinton.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac heaped praise on U.S. President Bill Clinton on Wednesday in an effusive "My dear Bill" message pledging closer cooperation with an old ally with whom ties have recently been prickly.
Analysts said, however, that Chirac's unusually warm note was aimed more at a domestic audience and predicted Washington and Paris would remain at odds on many global matters in coming years.
"I have just heard the joyful news...May I say that no one is more delighted than I am," the French leader wrote Clinton following his re-election victory.

"Your presence at the White House will guarantee us an American partner who is friendly, clear-sighted, competent, but also generous. I know that with your re-election the close relations between our two countries will become even closer."
Commentators agreed the note was the warmest -- and the only one written in English -- to be made public by the Elysee presidential palace since Chirac moved in 18 months ago.
In another first, the Elysee released a second, equally effusive message to Hillary Clinton from Chirac's wife.

"Jacques and I are really deeply happy at the thought that we shall be seeing you regularly in the coming years," Bernadette Chirac wrote. The four had dined together at a posh Paris restaurant in June after a G7 industrial powers summit in Lyon.

"Chirac wants to show he has a warm and close personal relationship with Clinton, but a personal relationship is not the same thing as foreign policy," said Pascal Boniface, head of France's Institute for International and Strategic Relations.

"There have been numerous major policy differences in the recent past, and there will be more confrontations in the future," said Boniface, who nonetheless joked that Chirac's note sounded like "a declaration of love".
The note showed Chirac's desire to renew the style of the presidency in France, agreed commentator Olivier Duhamel.
"Chirac wants a warmer image for France's president," Duhamel said. He added, however, that the message's tone "can't be bad" for Franco-American ties.

Chirac, who won a seven-year term in 1995, is personally strongly pro-American, speaks fluent English, worked as a young man at a Howard Johnson's restaurant in the United States and even had a brief romance with a Texan belle.

The first leader of a major democracy elected to lead his country into the new millennium, Chirac even picked up in his message on one of Clinton's campaign themes, saying he was "glad that it falls upon you to build the bridge to the 21st century that you envision for the United States of America".
Opinion polls in France had shown that Clinton was overwhelmingly favoured by French citizens over Dole.
But they also found the French increasingly disenchanted with the United States, believing it to be too influential in the world and scarred by violence.
French officials, who have expressed irritation in recent months at U.S. policy in the Middle East and Africa, predicted few changes in U.S. policy goals abroad.

Foreign Minister Herve de Charette, who once said Paris "irritated" Washington in the Middle East, told France-Inter radio he thought Clinton would turn more towards foreign policy in his second term than in his first.
Ex-president Valery Giscard d'Estaing, who ruled from 1974 to 1981, predicted that Washington would become more self-assured abroad and increasingly unwilling to share responsibility with its allies.
In international policy "they want to act all alone, they want to solve the problems of the Middle East, they don't accept intervention by others," Giscard d'Estaing told RTL radio.
